phrases: Avraham Avinu approaches the Akeidah with far more than his own life at stake. Yitzchak is his beloved son, the child of the Divine promise, and the one through whom his avodah is meant to continue. Everything Avraham has built seems bound up with this child. Yet he is prepared to place even that future before Hashem.

Read together, Rav Tzadok HaKohen and the Beis Yaakov reveal several layers of this mesiras nefesh. Avraham gives up his claim to personal comfort and reward; he places the future of his avodah in Hashem's hands; and he yields the demand that he understand how Hashem's command and promise fit together. The Akeidah brings the deepest part of the self into the service of Hashem.

Avraham had already shown at Ur Kasdim that his love for Hashem could carry him through the prospect of death. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes the furnace from the Akeidah. A person may be prepared to die while knowing that his deepest hopes will survive him. At the Akeidah, Avraham was prepared to surrender what was dearer to him than his own continued life.
וְכֵן קִיֵּם מִקּוֹדֶם בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ בְּנִסָּיוֹן הַכִּבְשָׁן
He had already fulfilled with all your soul in the trial of the furnace.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִסָּיוֹן הָעֲקֵדָה נִקְרָא וּבְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ
Afterward, the trial of the Akeidah was called with all your might,
שֶׁמּוֹרֶה אַף דָּבָר שֶׁחָבִיב עָלָיו מְאֹד יוֹתֵר מִנַּפְשׁוֹ.
which includes even something exceedingly dear to him, more than his own life.

The words bechol meodecha reach into everything that a person calls his own. In Avraham's case, that included Yitzchak and the future entrusted to him. His mesiras nefesh reached the place where a person feels that the entire meaning of his life is being asked of him.

The Beis Yaakov states this with extraordinary clarity. Yitzchak was the very essence of Avraham's Olam Haba. He was the beloved son through whom the covenant would continue. Avraham was prepared to give even this good to Hashem, without reserving a spiritual possession that must remain his own.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהָעֲקֵידָה שֶׁרָצָה לְהַקְרִיב בְּנוֹ יְחִידוֹ אֲשֶׁר אֲהָבוֹ עוֹלָה כָּלִיל לַהַשֵּׁם,
As he did at the Akeidah, when he desired to offer his only son, whom he loved, as a complete burnt offering to Hashem,
וְאַף שֶׁזֹּאת הִיא עִיקַּר עוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁלּוֹ,
and although this was the very essence of his World to Come,
עִם כָּל זֶה רָצָה גַּם בְּזוֹ הַטּוֹבָה לַעֲבוֹד בִּפְעוּלַת הַשֵּׁם
nevertheless, he wished to devote even this good to Hashem's service,
וְאַף שֶׁלֹּא יִשָּׁאֵר לוֹ כְּלוּם.
even if nothing would remain for himself.

This describes Avraham's readiness to surrender; it does not say that Hashem ultimately took away his Olam Haba. The depth of the avodah lies in what he was willing to place before Hashem. His service did not depend on an assurance that his own spiritual future would emerge in a form he could recognize.

Kedushas Shabbos brings us to a still more searching point. The Satan challenges Avraham with the claim that he will ultimately be held guilty of shedding his son's blood. Rav Tzadok explains Avraham's response as a readiness to serve even against the hypothetical possibility of punishment. His intention is to bring Hashem nachas ruach.
וַאֲפִילּוּ יִהְיֶה אֱמֶת שֶׁיֵּעָנֵשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ עַל זֶה.
Even if it should be true that he will afterward be punished for this,
הוּא רוֹצֶה רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְלֹא לְקַבָּלַת שָׂכָר.
he desires only to perform all his actions for the sake of Heaven, without seeking to receive reward.
וַאֲפִילּוּ יֵעָנֵשׁ עַל זֶה הוּא מִתְכַּוֵּין לַעֲשׂוֹת נַחַת רוּחַ לְפָנָיו
Even if he should be punished for it, his intention is to bring Him nachas ruach,

A person can leave behind many material desires while still holding tightly to the spiritual benefit he expects from his avodah. These sources ask him to examine that attachment as well. Avraham's desire is that Hashem's will be fulfilled. Even the anticipated reward of the servant is placed in the hands of the One he serves.

Rav Tzadok explains in Toldos and Pesach that Avraham's ahavah could have supplied a powerful argument for preserving Yitzchak. Through Yitzchak, Hashem's Divinity would become known in the world. Avraham could have understood that future as the very purpose of his life's work. His yirah made him examine whether even this spiritual argument was being influenced by his love for his son.
אַךְ מִיִּרְאָתוֹ הַמּוּפְלֶגֶת יָרֵא לַעֲבוֹר פִּי הַשֵּׁם
But because of his extraordinary awe, he feared to transgress Hashem's word,

כִּי אַף שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ,
For although He had told him: So shall your offspring be,
וְנֶאֱמַר לוֹ אֶת בְּרִיתִי אָקִים אֶת יִצְחָק,
and he had been told: I shall establish My covenant with Yitzchak,
וְעַכְשָׁיו כְּשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ הַעֲלֵהוּ לְעוֹלָה
and now he was told: Bring him up as a burnt offering,
עִם כָּל זֶה הֶאֱמִין בַּדְּבָרִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים כְּמוֹ מִקֹּדֶם וְלֹא נָפְלוּ אֶצְלוֹ,
nevertheless he believed in the earlier statements just as before, and they did not lose their standing for him.
וְזֹאת הָאֱמוּנָה אֵין בְּשֵׂכֶל הָאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג,
This faith is beyond the grasp of human understanding.

Avraham's emunah holds the promise and the command together while their reconciliation remains hidden from him. He entrusts the future to Hashem. Giving up everything includes yielding the demand that the whole picture become clear to me before I can serve with a complete heart.

The Sfas Emes brings this avodah into the meaning of the word nefesh itself. Nefesh means will. The inner direction of mesiras nefesh is that a person's will becomes devoted to the ratzon of the Borei.
לִהְיוֹת כָּל רְצוֹנוֹ תָּמִיד רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא וְאֵין לוֹ דָּבָר אַחֵר בָּעוֹלָם
that his entire will should always be only to fulfill the Creator's will, with nothing else in his world.
זֶה מִקְּרֵי מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הוּא רָצוֹן
This is called mesiras nefesh, for nefesh means will,
וְעַל יְדֵי מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בְּפוֹעַל זוֹכִין לְזֶה הָרָצוֹן.
and through actual mesiras nefesh one merits this will.

This gives us a way to approach the Akeidah in ordinary life. A mitzvah may ask for time that I wanted to keep, honesty that carries a financial cost, tzedakah without recognition, or patience when I want to insist on my own way. In each case, something within the self can be offered to Hashem. The Beis Yaakov explicitly connects a mitzvah performed without an ulterior motive to Akeidas Yitzchak.
וְאִם עוֹשֶׂה מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם בְּלִי שׁוּם פְּנִיָּה רַק לִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
If he performs Hashem's mitzvah without any ulterior motive, solely for Hashem's will,

then the act reaches higher and higher,
שֶׁהָיָה לָהּ אֲחִיזָה בַּעֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק,
so that it has a connection to Akeidas Yitzchak.

The conclusion of the Akeidah completes this understanding. Avraham must now hear Hashem's command to stop. The same surrender of will that brought him up the mountain requires him to receive Yitzchak back as Hashem directs.
אַל תִּשְׁלַח יָדְךָ אֶל הַנַּעַר וְאַל תַּעַשׂ לוֹ מְאוּמָה
Do not stretch out your hand against the lad, and do nothing to him.

The avodah is complete devotion to the ratzon Hashem, through the giving and through the receiving. Yitzchak remains alive, and Avraham continues to serve with the gift that has been entrusted to him.

For us, the deeper meaning of giving up everything is to bring every part of life into that devotion: our comforts, our plans, our need for recognition, our hopes for spiritual achievement, and our insistence on understanding the outcome. We ask that all of them find their proper place in the service of Hashem. That is the Akeidah we carry into the avodah of this week.

phrases: Samael challenges Avraham with the claim that he will ultimately be held guilty of shedding his son's blood. This is the Midrash explained in the following passage of Kedushas Shabbos.
אָמַר לוֹ לְמָחָר אוֹמֵר לְךָ שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּם אַתְּ חַיָּב שֶׁשָּׁפַכְתָּ דָּמוֹ שֶׁל בִּנְךָ,
He said to him: Tomorrow He will say to you, You are a shedder of blood; you are liable for having shed your son's blood.
אָמַר לוֹ, עַל מְנָת כֵּן.
Avraham answered him: Even on that condition.

Rav Tzadok explains Avraham's response to the Satan. The statement concerns the Akeidah and explicitly accepts the hypothetical possibility of punishment; the words Olam Haba do not occur in this selected statement.
וְהוּא הֵשִׁיב עַל מְנָת כֵּן,
And he answered: Even on that condition,
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם כַּוָּנָתוֹ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְעוֹשֶׂה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ.
for in any event his intention is for the sake of Heaven, and he acts in the manner of a transgression undertaken for Heaven's sake.
וַאֲפִילּוּ יִהְיֶה אֱמֶת שֶׁיֵּעָנֵשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ עַל זֶה.
Even if it should be true that he will afterward be punished for this,
הוּא רוֹצֶה רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְלֹא לְקַבָּלַת שָׂכָר.
he desires only to perform all his actions for the sake of Heaven, without seeking to receive reward.
וַאֲפִילּוּ יֵעָנֵשׁ עַל זֶה הוּא מִתְכַּוֵּין לַעֲשׂוֹת נַחַת רוּחַ לְפָנָיו
Even if he should be punished for it, his intention is to bring Him nachas ruach,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּהֵיפֶךְ כַּוָּנָתוֹ לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ.
whereas, in taking the opposite course, his intention would be directed toward his love for his son.
The first excerpt refers to the fiery furnace. Later in the same maamar, Rav Tzadok explains the Akeidah through Avraham's yirah and his readiness to obey beyond his understanding.
וְרַק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבָּעֲרָה בּוֹ אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם מָסַר נַפְשׁוֹ וְנִשְׁמָתוֹ גַּם כֵּן
It was only because love of Hashem burned within him that he surrendered his life and his soul as well,
וְאַף שֶׁיַּפְסִיד חַס וְשָׁלוֹם חֶלְקוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא מַה בְּכָךְ
and even if, Heaven forbid, he should lose his portion in the World to Come, what of it?
כֵּיוָן שֶׁרְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁיִּתְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עַל יָדוֹ וְיִתְפַּרְסֵם אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ.
For his desire was that the Name of Heaven be sanctified through him, and that His Divinity, blessed be His Name, become known.
אַךְ אָז הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה בְּהַפְלָגָה
But then he exercised the attribute of awe to an extraordinary degree,
וְנִתְיָירֵא לַעֲבוֹר עַל רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
and feared to transgress His blessed will,
וְחָשַׁד אֶת עַצְמוֹ פֶּן הוּא נוֹגֵעַ מַה בַּדָּבָר לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ
suspecting that perhaps his love for his son gave him some personal interest in the matter.
וְאָז נִתְכַּלֵּל בְּאֶשָּׁא מִדַּת יִצְחָק
He was then encompassed within the fire, the attribute of Yitzchak.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּנִסָּיוֹן הָעֲקֵידָה עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה וְגוֹמֵר
This is what is stated in the trial of the Akeidah: Now I know that you fear God, and so forth
וְנִתְבָּאֵר תּוֹלְדוֹת מַאֲמָר א׳ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל וּמַסִּיק
as explained in Toldos, maamar 1, in the passage beginning Umasik.
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָמַר מַה לִּי אִם אֵינִי מֵבִין כֵּיוָן שֶׁכָּךְ צוּוֵּיתִי אֲנִי מְחוּיָּב לִשְׁמוֹעַ.
That is, he said: What does it matter that I do not understand? Since I have been commanded in this way, I am obligated to obey.

Rav Tzadok first explains that Avraham's ahavah could have supplied an argument for preserving Yitzchak so that Hashem's Divinity would continue to be proclaimed through him. The following sentence explains why Avraham would not rely on that argument.
אַךְ מִיִּרְאָתוֹ הַמּוּפְלֶגֶת יָרֵא לַעֲבוֹר פִּי הַשֵּׁם
But because of his extraordinary awe, he feared to transgress Hashem's word,
שֶׁחָשַׁד אֶת עַצְמוֹ פֶּן הוּא נוֹגֵעַ מַה בַּדָּבָר לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ.
suspecting that perhaps his love for his son gave him some personal interest in the matter.

Immediately before this excerpt, Rav Tzadok explicitly describes Avraham's willingness at the furnace to surrender his life and his share in Olam Haba. He then tests what that same ahavah might have suggested at the Akeidah, and shows its completion through yirah.
וְכֵן עַל פִּי מִדַּת אַהֲבָה זוֹ הָיָה צָרִיךְ לַעֲבוֹר עַל מִצְוַת עֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק.
Likewise, according to this attribute of love, he would have had reason to transgress the command of Akeidas Yitzchak,
כֵּיוָן שֶׁיָּדַע כִּי בְיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע
since he knew: Through Yitzchak shall offspring be called yours,
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ יִתְפַּרְסֵם אֱלֹקִיתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
meaning that through him His blessed Divinity would become known.
וְלֹא רָצָה שֶׁאֱלִיעֶזֶר יִהְיֶה הַמְפַרְסֵם אֱלֹקִיתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
He did not want Eliezer to be the one who would proclaim His blessed Divinity,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר וּבֶן מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי הוּא דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר,
as he said: And the steward of my household is Eliezer of Damascus.
אַךְ מִפְּנֵי יִרְאָתוֹ הָעֲצוּמָה לַעֲבוֹר עַל מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם
But because of his tremendous fear of transgressing Hashem's command,
שֶׁמָּא יֵשׁ לוֹ נְגִיעָה לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ
lest his love for his son be influencing him,
עַל פִּי מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה הַזּוֹ עָקַד אֶת יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ,
he bound his son Yitzchak in accordance with this attribute of awe.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹקִים אַתָּה וְלֹא חָשַׂכְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר.
This is what is stated: For now I know that you fear God, and you have not withheld, and so forth.
וְאָז נִשְׁלַם בְּמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה כְּשֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי יִרְאָה,
His attribute of love was then brought to completion when it came through awe.
This passage explicitly distinguishes the furnace from the Akeidah. It describes surrendering what is more precious than one's own life, without explicitly using the words Olam Haba.
וְכֵן קִיֵּם מִקּוֹדֶם בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ בְּנִסָּיוֹן הַכִּבְשָׁן
He had already fulfilled with all your soul in the trial of the furnace.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִסָּיוֹן הָעֲקֵדָה נִקְרָא וּבְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ
Afterward, the trial of the Akeidah was called with all your might,
שֶׁמּוֹרֶה אַף דָּבָר שֶׁחָבִיב עָלָיו מְאֹד יוֹתֵר מִנַּפְשׁוֹ.
which includes even something exceedingly dear to him, more than his own life.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם שִׁבְּחוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּבְחִינַת יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים
Nevertheless, Hashem praised him as one who fears God,
מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאָז עָשָׂה מִצְוַת הָאַהֲבָה בְּכֹחַ וּגְבוּרָה
because then he fulfilled the mitzvah of love with strength and might,
שֶׁבָּעַר בּוֹ הָאַהֲבָה בְּשַׁלְהֶבֶת יָהּ.
as love burned within him with a flame of God.

This opening statement extends mesiras nefesh beyond its ordinary literal sense. Rav Tzadok then cites the Zohar's inclusion of nefesh, ruach and neshamah, and develops examples involving love of Hashem, Torah and Israel. The selected sentence itself does not explicitly mention forfeiting Olam Haba.
מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם
Mesiras nefesh out of love for Hashem
אֵינוֹ הַנֶּפֶשׁ לְבַד כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ
does not mean one's life alone in the literal sense,
אֶלָּא גַּם הַנְּשָׁמָה.
but also the neshamah.

The Izhbitzer explains why the first paragraph of Shema says with all your might, while the second does not. His qualification concerning a person's clarified spiritual portion is retained in the excerpt.
וּבְפָרָשַׁת וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ לֹא נֶאֱמַר וּבְכָל מְאֹדֵיכֶם,
In the paragraph Vehayah im shamoa, it does not say with all your might,
כִּי מְאֹדֶךָ הַיְינוּ מְאֹד מְאֹד לִמְסוֹר אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ עַל קְדֻשַּׁת שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
for meodecha means an exceedingly great surrender of one's soul for the sanctification of His blessed Name,
הַיְינוּ לִמְסוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ אַף בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא;
meaning to surrender oneself even with respect to life in the World to Come.
וְזֶהוּ רַק קוֹדֶם שֶׁיִּתְבָּרֵר לָאָדָם חֶלְקוֹ הַשַּׁיָּךְ לוֹ בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ,
This applies only before the portion belonging to a person at his root has become clear to him,
כִּי לְכָל נֶפֶשׁ שַׁיָּךְ מִצְוָה מְיוּחֶדֶת
for to every soul there belongs a particular mitzvah
שֶׁעַל יָדָהּ יַגִּיעַ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּפִי הַמִּצְוָה וּכְפִי אֲשֶׁר יְקַיְּמֶהָ,
through which that soul will attain the World to Come, according to the mitzvah and the manner in which he fulfills it,
וְזֶה עִיקָּר לְכָל נֶפֶשׁ;
and this is fundamental for each soul.
וְקוֹדֶם שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר לָאָדָם חֶלְקוֹ צָרִיךְ לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַשֵּׁם בְּזֶה הָאוֹפֶן
Before his portion has become clear to him, a person must serve Hashem in this manner:
שֶׁלֹּא יִמָּצֵא אֶצְלוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לְמָסְרָהּ עַל קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם;
that there be nothing in his possession which he would be unable to surrender for Kiddush Hashem.
אַךְ אַחַר שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר לָאָדָם חֶלְקוֹ
But after a person's portion has been clarified,
לֹא יַחְפּוֹץ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִן הָאָדָם שֶׁיַּעֲבוֹד אוֹתוֹ בְּזֶה הָאוֹפֶן,
Hashem does not desire that he serve Him in this manner,
כִּי לֹא יִרְצֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִיקַּח מִן הָאָדָם מַה שֶּׁסִּיגֵּל;
for Hashem does not wish to take from a person what he has acquired.

The Izhbitzer interprets the aravah, which has neither taste nor fragrance, as a necessary dimension of spiritual completeness. His concluding statement that Hashem will restore what was lost is included.
עַרְבֵי נָחַל הוּא נֶגֶד עוֹמֶק רָע, כִּי אֵין בָּהּ לֹא טַעַם וְלֹא רֵיחַ;
The willows of the brook correspond to the depth of evil, for the willow has neither taste nor fragrance.
וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה כִּדְאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא:
The meaning is as stated in the Gemara:
כָּל הַמּוֹסֵר נַפְשׁוֹ לָמוּת עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֵין אוֹמְרִים דְּבַר הֲלָכָה מִשְּׁמוֹ, בָּבָא קַמָּא דַּף ס״א.
Whoever gives himself over to die for words of Torah, a halachic teaching is not stated in his name. Bava Kamma 61a.
וְנִרְאֶה שֶׁמִּזֶּה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה לֹא יַגִּיעַ לְהָאָדָם שׁוּם הֲנָאָה לֹא בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלֹא בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא;
It appears that from this act no benefit will reach the person, either in this world or in the World to Come.
אַךְ בְּהָאֲגוּדָּה מֵהַצּוֹרֶךְ גַּם עֲרָבָה לְהִמָּצֵא,
Yet the willow, too, must be present in the bundle,
כִּי אֲגוּדָּה רוֹמֵז עַל שְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם,
for the bundle alludes to the completeness of the person.
וּבִשְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם צָרִיךְ לְהִמָּצֵא גַּם הַכֹּחַ הַזֶּה
For the person's completeness, this capacity must also be present:
שֶׁיּוּכַל לִמְסוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ לָמוּת אַף שֶׁלֹּא יַגִּיעַ לוֹ הֲנָאָה אַף לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא;
that he be able to surrender his life unto death even if no benefit will reach him, even in the World to Come.
וּבְאִם יִמָּצֵא בָּאָדָם זֶה הַכֹּחַ אָז יַשִּׂיג גַּם שְׁאָר הָעוֹמָקִים בִּשְׁלֵימוּת,
If this capacity is present in a person, he will then attain the other depths in their completeness as well.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִקָּרֵא עוֹמֶק, לְפִי שֶׁגַּם בְּהָרַע יִמָּצֵא טוֹב
Through this it is called a depth, because good will be found even within the evil,
וְהִיא שֶׁלֶּעָתִיד יַחֲזוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְכָל מִי שֶׁהִפְסִיד בִּמְסִירוּת נַפְשׁוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
namely, that in the future Hashem will restore to everyone what he lost through surrendering his life for words of Torah.
This is the most explicit direct connection between the Akeidah and giving up Olam Haba. Beis Yaakov then extends the principle to an ordinary mitzvah performed entirely for Hashem.
וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה, כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
The meaning is that Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him,
הִנִּיחַ וְעָזַב כָּל חֶמְדַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְאַף חַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא
set aside and relinquished everything desirable in this world, and even the life of the World to Come,
בִּכְדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לַאֲתַר דְּלָא אִתְיְידַע,
in order to fulfill Hashem's will, reaching the realm that is not known.
וּפְעוּלָה כָּזוֹ הִגִּיעָה לְרוּם הַמַּעֲלוֹת עַד לְעַתִּיקָא קַדִּישָׁא.
Such an act reached the loftiest heights, as far as Atika Kadisha.
וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָבַד לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַף בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא גַּם כֵּן,
Avraham Avinu served Hashem with even the life of the World to Come as well,
וְכָעִנְיָן דְּאִיתָא תַּנְחוּמָא לֶךְ ג׳
in keeping with what is stated in Tanchuma, Lech Lecha 3:
נִסָּיוֹן הָרִאשׁוֹן כְּנִסָּיוֹן הָאַחֲרוֹן.
The first trial was like the last trial.
נִסָּיוֹן הָאַחֲרוֹן בְּלֶךְ לְךָ וְנִסָּיוֹן הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּלֶךְ לְךָ,
The last trial was introduced with lech lecha, and the first trial was introduced with lech lecha.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהָעֲקֵידָה שֶׁרָצָה לְהַקְרִיב בְּנוֹ יְחִידוֹ אֲשֶׁר אֲהָבוֹ עוֹלָה כָּלִיל לַהַשֵּׁם,
As he did at the Akeidah, when he desired to offer his only son, whom he loved, as a complete burnt offering to Hashem,
וְאַף שֶׁזֹּאת הִיא עִיקַּר עוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁלּוֹ,
and although this was the very essence of his World to Come,
עִם כָּל זֶה רָצָה גַּם בְּזוֹ הַטּוֹבָה לַעֲבוֹד בִּפְעוּלַת הַשֵּׁם
nevertheless, he wished to devote even this good to Hashem's service,
וְאַף שֶׁלֹּא יִשָּׁאֵר לוֹ כְּלוּם.
even if nothing would remain for himself.
אַף כִּי אִיתָא רַבָּה לֶךְ מ״ד שֶׁהִבְטִיחַ לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שְׂכָרְךָ מְתוּקָּן לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא,
Although it is stated in Bereishis Rabbah, Lech Lecha 44, that the Holy One, blessed be He, promised him, Your reward is prepared for the future,
אָכֵן אֵין נִרְאֶה זֹאת לָעַיִן וְלֹא נוֹדַע לָאָדָם.
this is nevertheless not visible to the eye and is not known to the person.
וְאִם עוֹשֶׂה מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם בְּלִי שׁוּם פְּנִיָּה רַק לִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
If he performs Hashem's mitzvah without any ulterior motive, solely for Hashem's will,
אָז נוֹגֵעַ הַפְּעוּלָה מַעְלָה מַעְלָה,
then the act reaches higher and higher,
שֶׁהָיָה לָהּ אֲחִיזָה בַּעֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק,
so that it has a connection to Akeidas Yitzchak.

Beis Yaakov states this spiritual ideal while explaining what Esav sought to convey through his question about tithing salt. The surrounding argument describes Esav's deceptive presentation to Yitzchak; it does not establish that Esav truly attained this avodah.
כִּי יֵשׁ גַּם עֲבוֹדָה גְּדוֹלָה מִזּוֹ
For there is also a greater form of service than this:
שֶׁהָאָדָם מוֹסֵר נַפְשׁוֹ בִּמְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּבָעוֹלָם הַבָּא בִּשְׁבִיל כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם,
that a person surrenders himself through mesiras nefesh in this world and in the World to Come for the honor of Heaven.
כִּי גַּם כַּוָּנָה לִשְׂכַר בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְגַרְמֵיהּ;
For even an intention directed toward the reward of the World to Come is also for oneself.
This passage adds a distinct dimension: Avraham retained his faith in Hashem's earlier promises even while proceeding with the Akeidah. It does not explicitly state that he forfeited Olam Haba.
וְהָאֱלֹקִים נִסָּה אֶת אַבְרָהָם.
And God tested Avraham.
עִנְיַן נִסָּיוֹן שֶׁל הָעֲקֵדָה הָיָה גֹּדֶל הָאֱמוּנָה שֶׁהָיָה לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
The matter tested at the Akeidah was the greatness of Avraham Avinu's faith in Hashem.
כִּי אַף שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ,
For although He had told him: So shall your offspring be,
וְנֶאֱמַר לוֹ אֶת בְּרִיתִי אָקִים אֶת יִצְחָק,
and he had been told: I shall establish My covenant with Yitzchak,
וְעַכְשָׁיו כְּשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ הַעֲלֵהוּ לְעוֹלָה
and now he was told: Bring him up as a burnt offering,
עִם כָּל זֶה הֶאֱמִין בַּדְּבָרִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים כְּמוֹ מִקֹּדֶם וְלֹא נָפְלוּ אֶצְלוֹ,
nevertheless he believed in the earlier statements just as before, and they did not lose their standing for him.
וְזֹאת הָאֱמוּנָה אֵין בְּשֵׂכֶל הָאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג,
This faith is beyond the grasp of human understanding.
This additional Chassidic parallel explicitly states the general principle and illustrates it through Rochel giving Leah the identifying signs, despite the future she believed she might lose.
הַכְּלָל הוּא שֶׁאָדָם צָרִיךְ לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַבּוֹרֵא בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֹא בִּשְׁבִיל שׁוּם קַבָּלַת שָׂכָר כְּלָל
The principle is that a person must serve the Creator, blessed be He, without seeking any reward at all,
וְיִמְסוֹר עַצְמוֹ הֵן חֶלְקוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְהֵן חֶלְקוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא
and surrender himself, both his portion in this world and his portion in the World to Come, in order to fulfill the Creator's will.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּרָחֵל שֶׁעָשְׂתָה הַמִּצְוָה לִמְסוֹר הַסִּימָנִים לְלֵאָה
As we find with Rochel, who performed the mitzvah of handing over the identifying signs to Leah,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה שׁוּב לֹא יִשָּׂא אוֹתָהּ יַעֲקֹב וְתַעֲלֶה אֶל גּוֹרָלוֹ שֶׁל עֵשָׂו כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
even though, through this, Yaakov would no longer marry her and she would fall to Esav's lot, as stated above.
וְנִמְצָא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם תֹּאבַד חֶלְקָהּ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּשֶׁיִּשָּׂא אוֹתָהּ עֵשָׂו חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
It would follow, Heaven forbid, that she would lose her portion in the World to Come if Esav were to marry her, Heaven forbid.
אַף עַל פִּי כֵן מָסְרָה הַסִּימָנִים
Nevertheless, she handed over the signs,
וּמָסְרָה עַצְמָהּ הֵן חֶלְקָהּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֵן בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא
and surrendered herself, both her portion in this world and in the World to Come,
בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא.
in order that the Creator's will be fulfilled.

The Bnei Yissaschar develops this within his explanation of Yosef's reasoning about Avraham's status. The excerpt concerns the furnace, and expressly speaks of Avraham accepting even the prospect of punishment in Olam Haba.
וְיוֹסֵף הָיָה סוֹבֵר דְּשָׁאנֵי אַבְרָהָם דַּהֲרֵי מָסַר אֶת עַצְמוֹ עַל קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם,
Yosef held that Avraham was different, for he had surrendered himself for Kiddush Hashem,
וְהוּא שֶׁלֹּא כְתוֹרָה לְבֶן נֹחַ דְּאֵינוֹ מְצוּוֶה עַל קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם,
which was not in accordance with the law of a descendant of Noach, who is not commanded in Kiddush Hashem,
וְאַדְּרַבָּא מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּאַךְ אֶת דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם וְכוּלֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית ט׳ ה׳,
and, on the contrary, incurs liability under But your blood, of your lives, and so forth, Bereishis 9:5.
אַךְ אַבְרָהָם בַּעֲבוּר קְדוּשַּׁת שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מָסַר אֶת עַצְמוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּבָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
Yet Avraham, for the sanctification of His blessed Name, surrendered himself in this world and in the World to Come,
כִּי הָיָה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁיֵּעָנֵשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא עַל מְסִירוּת נַפְשׁוֹ,
for he thought that he would be punished in the World to Come for surrendering his life.
וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן הִשְׁלִיךְ אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ מִנֶּגֶד עֲבוּר אַהֲבָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר כָּתַבְנוּ בִּמְקוֹמוֹ,
Nevertheless, he cast his life aside out of love for Him, blessed be His Name, as we explained in its place.
וְאִם כֵּן דִּין הוּא שֶׁיֵּצֵא מִכְּלַל בֶּן נֹחַ לְגַמְרֵי, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַבָּנִים, וְהָבֵן.
If so, it is fitting that he should leave the status of a descendant of Noach entirely, unlike the children; understand this.

This additional parallel explains the meaning of nefesh as will, and connects Avraham's mesiras nefesh to service without expectation of reward. It speaks of unconditioned love rather than explicitly forfeiting Olam Haba.
כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁמָּסַר נַפְשׁוֹ לִשְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
For Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, was the first to surrender his life for His blessed Name.
וּבֶאֱמֶת בִּמְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ זוֹכִין אֶל זֶה הַזְּרִיזוּת
Through mesiras nefesh, one truly merits this alacrity:
לִהְיוֹת כָּל רְצוֹנוֹ תָּמִיד רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא וְאֵין לוֹ דָּבָר אַחֵר בָּעוֹלָם
that his entire will should always be only to fulfill the Creator's will, with nothing else in his world.
זֶה מִקְּרֵי מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הוּא רָצוֹן
This is called mesiras nefesh, for nefesh means will,
וְעַל יְדֵי מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בְּפוֹעַל זוֹכִין לְזֶה הָרָצוֹן.
and through actual mesiras nefesh one merits this will.
אָכֵן תַּלְמִידֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לִהְיוֹת עוֹבֵד הַשֵּׁם שֶׁלֹּא עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס רַק לִשְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּלְבַד.
The disciples of Avraham Avinu, however, seek to serve Hashem without the intention of receiving reward, solely for His blessed Name.
וּמְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ הוּא עֵדוּת עַל זֶה שֶׁהִיא שֶׁלֹּא עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס
Mesiras nefesh testifies that this service is without the intention of receiving reward,
כִּי מִי שֶׁמּוֹסֵר נַפְשׁוֹ וּמְאוֹדוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם הִיא אַהֲבָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ תְּלוּיָה בְּדָבָר
for when someone surrenders his life and his resources to Heaven, this is a love independent of any condition,
וְלָכֵן אֵינָהּ בְּטֵילָה לְעוֹלָם.
and therefore it never ceases.

he: אָמַר לוֹ לְמָחָר אוֹמֵר לְךָ שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּם אַתְּ חַיָּב שֶׁשָּׁפַכְתָּ דָּמוֹ שֶׁל בִּנְךָ, אָמַר לוֹ, עַל מְנָת כֵּן.

וְהוּא הֵשִׁיב עַל מְנָת כֵּן, דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם כַּוָּנָתוֹ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְעוֹשֶׂה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ. וַאֲפִילּוּ יִהְיֶה אֱמֶת שֶׁיֵּעָנֵשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ עַל זֶה. הוּא רוֹצֶה רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְלֹא לְקַבָּלַת שָׂכָר. וַאֲפִילּוּ יֵעָנֵשׁ עַל זֶה הוּא מִתְכַּוֵּין לַעֲשׂוֹת נַחַת רוּחַ לְפָנָיו מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּהֵיפֶךְ כַּוָּנָתוֹ לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ.

וְרַק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבָּעֲרָה בּוֹ אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם מָסַר נַפְשׁוֹ וְנִשְׁמָתוֹ גַּם כֵּן וְאַף שֶׁיַּפְסִיד חַס וְשָׁלוֹם חֶלְקוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא מַה בְּכָךְ כֵּיוָן שֶׁרְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁיִּתְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עַל יָדוֹ וְיִתְפַּרְסֵם אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ.

אַךְ אָז הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה בְּהַפְלָגָה וְנִתְיָירֵא לַעֲבוֹר עַל רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְחָשַׁד אֶת עַצְמוֹ פֶּן הוּא נוֹגֵעַ מַה בַּדָּבָר לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ וְאָז נִתְכַּלֵּל בְּאֶשָּׁא מִדַּת יִצְחָק וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּנִסָּיוֹן הָעֲקֵידָה עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה וְגוֹמֵר וְנִתְבָּאֵר תּוֹלְדוֹת מַאֲמָר א׳ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל וּמַסִּיק וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָמַר מַה לִּי אִם אֵינִי מֵבִין כֵּיוָן שֶׁכָּךְ צוּוֵּיתִי אֲנִי מְחוּיָּב לִשְׁמוֹעַ.
אַךְ מִיִּרְאָתוֹ הַמּוּפְלֶגֶת יָרֵא לַעֲבוֹר פִּי הַשֵּׁם שֶׁחָשַׁד אֶת עַצְמוֹ פֶּן הוּא נוֹגֵעַ מַה בַּדָּבָר לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ.

וְכֵן עַל פִּי מִדַּת אַהֲבָה זוֹ הָיָה צָרִיךְ לַעֲבוֹר עַל מִצְוַת עֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק. כֵּיוָן שֶׁיָּדַע כִּי בְיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ יִתְפַּרְסֵם אֱלֹקִיתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלֹא רָצָה שֶׁאֱלִיעֶזֶר יִהְיֶה הַמְפַרְסֵם אֱלֹקִיתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר וּבֶן מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי הוּא דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר, אַךְ מִפְּנֵי יִרְאָתוֹ הָעֲצוּמָה לַעֲבוֹר עַל מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם שֶׁמָּא יֵשׁ לוֹ נְגִיעָה לְאַהֲבַת בְּנוֹ עַל פִּי מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה הַזּוֹ עָקַד אֶת יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ, וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹקִים אַתָּה וְלֹא חָשַׂכְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר. וְאָז נִשְׁלַם בְּמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה כְּשֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי יִרְאָה,

וְכֵן קִיֵּם מִקּוֹדֶם בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ בְּנִסָּיוֹן הַכִּבְשָׁן וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִסָּיוֹן הָעֲקֵדָה נִקְרָא וּבְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ שֶׁמּוֹרֶה אַף דָּבָר שֶׁחָבִיב עָלָיו מְאֹד יוֹתֵר מִנַּפְשׁוֹ. וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם שִׁבְּחוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּבְחִינַת יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאָז עָשָׂה מִצְוַת הָאַהֲבָה בְּכֹחַ וּגְבוּרָה שֶׁבָּעַר בּוֹ הָאַהֲבָה בְּשַׁלְהֶבֶת יָהּ.
מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם אֵינוֹ הַנֶּפֶשׁ לְבַד כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ אֶלָּא גַּם הַנְּשָׁמָה.

וּבְפָרָשַׁת וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ לֹא נֶאֱמַר וּבְכָל מְאֹדֵיכֶם, כִּי מְאֹדֶךָ הַיְינוּ מְאֹד מְאֹד לִמְסוֹר אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ עַל קְדֻשַּׁת שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, הַיְינוּ לִמְסוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ אַף בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא; וְזֶהוּ רַק קוֹדֶם שֶׁיִּתְבָּרֵר לָאָדָם חֶלְקוֹ הַשַּׁיָּךְ לוֹ בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ, כִּי לְכָל נֶפֶשׁ שַׁיָּךְ מִצְוָה מְיוּחֶדֶת שֶׁעַל יָדָהּ יַגִּיעַ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּפִי הַמִּצְוָה וּכְפִי אֲשֶׁר יְקַיְּמֶהָ, וְזֶה עִיקָּר לְכָל נֶפֶשׁ; וְקוֹדֶם שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר לָאָדָם חֶלְקוֹ צָרִיךְ לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַשֵּׁם בְּזֶה הָאוֹפֶן שֶׁלֹּא יִמָּצֵא אֶצְלוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לְמָסְרָהּ עַל קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם; אַךְ אַחַר שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר לָאָדָם חֶלְקוֹ לֹא יַחְפּוֹץ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִן הָאָדָם שֶׁיַּעֲבוֹד אוֹתוֹ בְּזֶה הָאוֹפֶן, כִּי לֹא יִרְצֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִיקַּח מִן הָאָדָם מַה שֶּׁסִּיגֵּל;

עַרְבֵי נָחַל הוּא נֶגֶד עוֹמֶק רָע, כִּי אֵין בָּהּ לֹא טַעַם וְלֹא רֵיחַ; וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה כִּדְאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא: כָּל הַמּוֹסֵר נַפְשׁוֹ לָמוּת עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֵין אוֹמְרִים דְּבַר הֲלָכָה מִשְּׁמוֹ, בָּבָא קַמָּא דַּף ס״א. וְנִרְאֶה שֶׁמִּזֶּה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה לֹא יַגִּיעַ לְהָאָדָם שׁוּם הֲנָאָה לֹא בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלֹא בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא; אַךְ בְּהָאֲגוּדָּה מֵהַצּוֹרֶךְ גַּם עֲרָבָה לְהִמָּצֵא, כִּי אֲגוּדָּה רוֹמֵז עַל שְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם, וּבִשְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם צָרִיךְ לְהִמָּצֵא גַּם הַכֹּחַ הַזֶּה שֶׁיּוּכַל לִמְסוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ לָמוּת אַף שֶׁלֹּא יַגִּיעַ לוֹ הֲנָאָה אַף לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא; וּבְאִם יִמָּצֵא בָּאָדָם זֶה הַכֹּחַ אָז יַשִּׂיג גַּם שְׁאָר הָעוֹמָקִים בִּשְׁלֵימוּת, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִקָּרֵא עוֹמֶק, לְפִי שֶׁגַּם בְּהָרַע יִמָּצֵא טוֹב וְהִיא שֶׁלֶּעָתִיד יַחֲזוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְכָל מִי שֶׁהִפְסִיד בִּמְסִירוּת נַפְשׁוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.

וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה, כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִנִּיחַ וְעָזַב כָּל חֶמְדַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְאַף חַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא בִּכְדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לַאֲתַר דְּלָא אִתְיְידַע, וּפְעוּלָה כָּזוֹ הִגִּיעָה לְרוּם הַמַּעֲלוֹת עַד לְעַתִּיקָא קַדִּישָׁא.

וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָבַד לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַף בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא גַּם כֵּן, וְכָעִנְיָן דְּאִיתָא תַּנְחוּמָא לֶךְ ג׳ נִסָּיוֹן הָרִאשׁוֹן כְּנִסָּיוֹן הָאַחֲרוֹן. נִסָּיוֹן הָאַחֲרוֹן בְּלֶךְ לְךָ וְנִסָּיוֹן הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּלֶךְ לְךָ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהָעֲקֵידָה שֶׁרָצָה לְהַקְרִיב בְּנוֹ יְחִידוֹ אֲשֶׁר אֲהָבוֹ עוֹלָה כָּלִיל לַהַשֵּׁם, וְאַף שֶׁזֹּאת הִיא עִיקַּר עוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁלּוֹ, עִם כָּל זֶה רָצָה גַּם בְּזוֹ הַטּוֹבָה לַעֲבוֹד בִּפְעוּלַת הַשֵּׁם וְאַף שֶׁלֹּא יִשָּׁאֵר לוֹ כְּלוּם. אַף כִּי אִיתָא רַבָּה לֶךְ מ״ד שֶׁהִבְטִיחַ לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שְׂכָרְךָ מְתוּקָּן לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא, אָכֵן אֵין נִרְאֶה זֹאת לָעַיִן וְלֹא נוֹדַע לָאָדָם.
וְאִם עוֹשֶׂה מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם בְּלִי שׁוּם פְּנִיָּה רַק לִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אָז נוֹגֵעַ הַפְּעוּלָה מַעְלָה מַעְלָה, שֶׁהָיָה לָהּ אֲחִיזָה בַּעֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק,

כִּי יֵשׁ גַּם עֲבוֹדָה גְּדוֹלָה מִזּוֹ שֶׁהָאָדָם מוֹסֵר נַפְשׁוֹ בִּמְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּבָעוֹלָם הַבָּא בִּשְׁבִיל כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם, כִּי גַּם כַּוָּנָה לִשְׂכַר בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְגַרְמֵיהּ;

וְהָאֱלֹקִים נִסָּה אֶת אַבְרָהָם. עִנְיַן נִסָּיוֹן שֶׁל הָעֲקֵדָה הָיָה גֹּדֶל הָאֱמוּנָה שֶׁהָיָה לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי אַף שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ, וְנֶאֱמַר לוֹ אֶת בְּרִיתִי אָקִים אֶת יִצְחָק, וְעַכְשָׁיו כְּשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ הַעֲלֵהוּ לְעוֹלָה עִם כָּל זֶה הֶאֱמִין בַּדְּבָרִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים כְּמוֹ מִקֹּדֶם וְלֹא נָפְלוּ אֶצְלוֹ, וְזֹאת הָאֱמוּנָה אֵין בְּשֵׂכֶל הָאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג,

הַכְּלָל הוּא שֶׁאָדָם צָרִיךְ לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַבּוֹרֵא בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֹא בִּשְׁבִיל שׁוּם קַבָּלַת שָׂכָר כְּלָל וְיִמְסוֹר עַצְמוֹ הֵן חֶלְקוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְהֵן חֶלְקוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּרָחֵל שֶׁעָשְׂתָה הַמִּצְוָה לִמְסוֹר הַסִּימָנִים לְלֵאָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה שׁוּב לֹא יִשָּׂא אוֹתָהּ יַעֲקֹב וְתַעֲלֶה אֶל גּוֹרָלוֹ שֶׁל עֵשָׂו כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וְנִמְצָא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם תֹּאבַד חֶלְקָהּ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּשֶׁיִּשָּׂא אוֹתָהּ עֵשָׂו חַס וְשָׁלוֹם אַף עַל פִּי כֵן מָסְרָה הַסִּימָנִים וּמָסְרָה עַצְמָהּ הֵן חֶלְקָהּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֵן בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא.

וְיוֹסֵף הָיָה סוֹבֵר דְּשָׁאנֵי אַבְרָהָם דַּהֲרֵי מָסַר אֶת עַצְמוֹ עַל קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם, וְהוּא שֶׁלֹּא כְתוֹרָה לְבֶן נֹחַ דְּאֵינוֹ מְצוּוֶה עַל קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם, וְאַדְּרַבָּא מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּאַךְ אֶת דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם וְכוּלֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית ט׳ ה׳, אַךְ אַבְרָהָם בַּעֲבוּר קְדוּשַּׁת שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מָסַר אֶת עַצְמוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּבָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, כִּי הָיָה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁיֵּעָנֵשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא עַל מְסִירוּת נַפְשׁוֹ, וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן הִשְׁלִיךְ אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ מִנֶּגֶד עֲבוּר אַהֲבָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר כָּתַבְנוּ בִּמְקוֹמוֹ, וְאִם כֵּן דִּין הוּא שֶׁיֵּצֵא מִכְּלַל בֶּן נֹחַ לְגַמְרֵי, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַבָּנִים, וְהָבֵן.

כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁמָּסַר נַפְשׁוֹ לִשְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּבֶאֱמֶת בִּמְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ זוֹכִין אֶל זֶה הַזְּרִיזוּת לִהְיוֹת כָּל רְצוֹנוֹ תָּמִיד רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן הַבּוֹרֵא וְאֵין לוֹ דָּבָר אַחֵר בָּעוֹלָם זֶה מִקְּרֵי מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הוּא רָצוֹן וְעַל יְדֵי מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בְּפוֹעַל זוֹכִין לְזֶה הָרָצוֹן.

אָכֵן תַּלְמִידֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לִהְיוֹת עוֹבֵד הַשֵּׁם שֶׁלֹּא עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס רַק לִשְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּלְבַד. וּמְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ הוּא עֵדוּת עַל זֶה שֶׁהִיא שֶׁלֹּא עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס כִּי מִי שֶׁמּוֹסֵר נַפְשׁוֹ וּמְאוֹדוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם הִיא אַהֲבָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ תְּלוּיָה בְּדָבָר וְלָכֵן אֵינָהּ בְּטֵילָה לְעוֹלָם.
en: Samael challenges Avraham with the claim that he will ultimately be held guilty of shedding his son's blood. This is the Midrash explained in the following passage of Kedushas Shabbos.
He said to him: Tomorrow He will say to you, You are a shedder of blood; you are liable for having shed your son's blood. Avraham answered him: Even on that condition.

Rav Tzadok explains Avraham's response to the Satan. The statement concerns the Akeidah and explicitly accepts the hypothetical possibility of punishment; the words Olam Haba do not occur in this selected statement.

And he answered: Even on that condition, for in any event his intention is for the sake of Heaven, and he acts in the manner of a transgression undertaken for Heaven's sake. Even if it should be true that he will afterward be punished for this, he desires only to perform all his actions for the sake of Heaven, without seeking to receive reward. Even if he should be punished for it, his intention is to bring Him nachas ruach, whereas, in taking the opposite course, his intention would be directed toward his love for his son.
The first excerpt refers to the fiery furnace. Later in the same maamar, Rav Tzadok explains the Akeidah through Avraham's yirah and his readiness to obey beyond his understanding.

It was only because love of Hashem burned within him that he surrendered his life and his soul as well, and even if, Heaven forbid, he should lose his portion in the World to Come, what of it? For his desire was that the Name of Heaven be sanctified through him, and that His Divinity, blessed be His Name, become known.

But then he exercised the attribute of awe to an extraordinary degree, and feared to transgress His blessed will, suspecting that perhaps his love for his son gave him some personal interest in the matter. He was then encompassed within the fire, the attribute of Yitzchak. This is what is stated in the trial of the Akeidah: Now I know that you fear God, and so forth as explained in Toldos, maamar 1, in the passage beginning Umasik. That is, he said: What does it matter that I do not understand? Since I have been commanded in this way, I am obligated to obey.

Rav Tzadok first explains that Avraham's ahavah could have supplied an argument for preserving Yitzchak so that Hashem's Divinity would continue to be proclaimed through him. The following sentence explains why Avraham would not rely on that argument.
But because of his extraordinary awe, he feared to transgress Hashem's word, suspecting that perhaps his love for his son gave him some personal interest in the matter.

Immediately before this excerpt, Rav Tzadok explicitly describes Avraham's willingness at the furnace to surrender his life and his share in Olam Haba. He then tests what that same ahavah might have suggested at the Akeidah, and shows its completion through yirah.

Likewise, according to this attribute of love, he would have had reason to transgress the command of Akeidas Yitzchak, since he knew: Through Yitzchak shall offspring be called yours, meaning that through him His blessed Divinity would become known. He did not want Eliezer to be the one who would proclaim His blessed Divinity, as he said: And the steward of my household is Eliezer of Damascus. But because of his tremendous fear of transgressing Hashem's command, lest his love for his son be influencing him, he bound his son Yitzchak in accordance with this attribute of awe. This is what is stated: For now I know that you fear God, and you have not withheld, and so forth. His attribute of love was then brought to completion when it came through awe.
This passage explicitly distinguishes the furnace from the Akeidah. It describes surrendering what is more precious than one's own life, without explicitly using the words Olam Haba.

He had already fulfilled with all your soul in the trial of the furnace. Afterward, the trial of the Akeidah was called with all your might, which includes even something exceedingly dear to him, more than his own life. Nevertheless, Hashem praised him as one who fears God, because then he fulfilled the mitzvah of love with strength and might, as love burned within him with a flame of God.

This opening statement extends mesiras nefesh beyond its ordinary literal sense. Rav Tzadok then cites the Zohar's inclusion of nefesh, ruach and neshamah, and develops examples involving love of Hashem, Torah and Israel. The selected sentence itself does not explicitly mention forfeiting Olam Haba.
Mesiras nefesh out of love for Hashem does not mean one's life alone in the literal sense, but also the neshamah.

The Izhbitzer explains why the first paragraph of Shema says with all your might, while the second does not. His qualification concerning a person's clarified spiritual portion is retained in the excerpt.

In the paragraph Vehayah im shamoa, it does not say with all your might, for meodecha means an exceedingly great surrender of one's soul for the sanctification of His blessed Name, meaning to surrender oneself even with respect to life in the World to Come. This applies only before the portion belonging to a person at his root has become clear to him, for to every soul there belongs a particular mitzvah through which that soul will attain the World to Come, according to the mitzvah and the manner in which he fulfills it, and this is fundamental for each soul. Before his portion has become clear to him, a person must serve Hashem in this manner: that there be nothing in his possession which he would be unable to surrender for Kiddush Hashem. But after a person's portion has been clarified, Hashem does not desire that he serve Him in this manner, for Hashem does not wish to take from a person what he has acquired.

The Izhbitzer interprets the aravah, which has neither taste nor fragrance, as a necessary dimension of spiritual completeness. His concluding statement that Hashem will restore what was lost is included.

The willows of the brook correspond to the depth of evil, for the willow has neither taste nor fragrance. The meaning is as stated in the Gemara: Whoever gives himself over to die for words of Torah, a halachic teaching is not stated in his name. Bava Kamma 61a. It appears that from this act no benefit will reach the person, either in this world or in the World to Come. Yet the willow, too, must be present in the bundle, for the bundle alludes to the completeness of the person. For the person's completeness, this capacity must also be present: that he be able to surrender his life unto death even if no benefit will reach him, even in the World to Come. If this capacity is present in a person, he will then attain the other depths in their completeness as well. Through this it is called a depth, because good will be found even within the evil, namely, that in the future Hashem will restore to everyone what he lost through surrendering his life for words of Torah.
This is the most explicit direct connection between the Akeidah and giving up Olam Haba. Beis Yaakov then extends the principle to an ordinary mitzvah performed entirely for Hashem.

The meaning is that Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, set aside and relinquished everything desirable in this world, and even the life of the World to Come, in order to fulfill Hashem's will, reaching the realm that is not known. Such an act reached the loftiest heights, as far as Atika Kadisha.

Avraham Avinu served Hashem with even the life of the World to Come as well, in keeping with what is stated in Tanchuma, Lech Lecha 3: The first trial was like the last trial. The last trial was introduced with lech lecha, and the first trial was introduced with lech lecha. As he did at the Akeidah, when he desired to offer his only son, whom he loved, as a complete burnt offering to Hashem, and although this was the very essence of his World to Come, nevertheless, he wished to devote even this good to Hashem's service, even if nothing would remain for himself. Although it is stated in Bereishis Rabbah, Lech Lecha 44, that the Holy One, blessed be He, promised him, Your reward is prepared for the future, this is nevertheless not visible to the eye and is not known to the person.
If he performs Hashem's mitzvah without any ulterior motive, solely for Hashem's will, then the act reaches higher and higher, so that it has a connection to Akeidas Yitzchak.

Beis Yaakov states this spiritual ideal while explaining what Esav sought to convey through his question about tithing salt. The surrounding argument describes Esav's deceptive presentation to Yitzchak; it does not establish that Esav truly attained this avodah.

For there is also a greater form of service than this: that a person surrenders himself through mesiras nefesh in this world and in the World to Come for the honor of Heaven. For even an intention directed toward the reward of the World to Come is also for oneself.
This passage adds a distinct dimension: Avraham retained his faith in Hashem's earlier promises even while proceeding with the Akeidah. It does not explicitly state that he forfeited Olam Haba.

And God tested Avraham. The matter tested at the Akeidah was the greatness of Avraham Avinu's faith in Hashem. For although He had told him: So shall your offspring be, and he had been told: I shall establish My covenant with Yitzchak, and now he was told: Bring him up as a burnt offering, nevertheless he believed in the earlier statements just as before, and they did not lose their standing for him. This faith is beyond the grasp of human understanding.
This additional Chassidic parallel explicitly states the general principle and illustrates it through Rochel giving Leah the identifying signs, despite the future she believed she might lose.

The principle is that a person must serve the Creator, blessed be He, without seeking any reward at all, and surrender himself, both his portion in this world and his portion in the World to Come, in order to fulfill the Creator's will. As we find with Rochel, who performed the mitzvah of handing over the identifying signs to Leah, even though, through this, Yaakov would no longer marry her and she would fall to Esav's lot, as stated above. It would follow, Heaven forbid, that she would lose her portion in the World to Come if Esav were to marry her, Heaven forbid. Nevertheless, she handed over the signs, and surrendered herself, both her portion in this world and in the World to Come, in order that the Creator's will be fulfilled.

The Bnei Yissaschar develops this within his explanation of Yosef's reasoning about Avraham's status. The excerpt concerns the furnace, and expressly speaks of Avraham accepting even the prospect of punishment in Olam Haba.

Yosef held that Avraham was different, for he had surrendered himself for Kiddush Hashem, which was not in accordance with the law of a descendant of Noach, who is not commanded in Kiddush Hashem, and, on the contrary, incurs liability under But your blood, of your lives, and so forth, Bereishis 9:5. Yet Avraham, for the sanctification of His blessed Name, surrendered himself in this world and in the World to Come, for he thought that he would be punished in the World to Come for surrendering his life. Nevertheless, he cast his life aside out of love for Him, blessed be His Name, as we explained in its place. If so, it is fitting that he should leave the status of a descendant of Noach entirely, unlike the children; understand this.

This additional parallel explains the meaning of nefesh as will, and connects Avraham's mesiras nefesh to service without expectation of reward. It speaks of unconditioned love rather than explicitly forfeiting Olam Haba.

For Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, was the first to surrender his life for His blessed Name. Through mesiras nefesh, one truly merits this alacrity: that his entire will should always be only to fulfill the Creator's will, with nothing else in his world. This is called mesiras nefesh, for nefesh means will, and through actual mesiras nefesh one merits this will.

The disciples of Avraham Avinu, however, seek to serve Hashem without the intention of receiving reward, solely for His blessed Name. Mesiras nefesh testifies that this service is without the intention of receiving reward, for when someone surrenders his life and his resources to Heaven, this is a love independent of any condition, and therefore it never ceases.
